details:
**Blood Wedding**
Lorca's most frequently clued play (1933), the first of his Rural Trilogy. The Mother, whose husband and son were killed by the Félix family, sees her son the Groom marry the Bride. The Bride was once the lover of Leonardo Félix, now married to her cousin, and at the wedding she runs off with Leonardo on horseback. The Groom chases them into the forest, where Leonardo and the Groom kill each other with knives.

**The Moon and Death as a Beggar Woman**
Symbolic characters in the forest scene of Blood Wedding's last act, which opens with three woodcutters. The Moon, played as a young woodcutter with a white face, longs for blood and promises to light the lovers' way. Death appears as a Beggar Woman and orders the Moon to give light so that "the knives will know the road."

**"Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías" and "at five in the afternoon"**
Lorca's famous 1935 elegy for his friend, the bullfighter Ignacio Sánchez Mejías, who died in 1934 after being gored. Its first section, "The Goring and the Death," repeats "at five in the afternoon" as a refrain after almost every line, including "A boy brought the white sheet" and "a basket of lime already prepared." The poem is also known in English as "Lament for the Death of a Bullfighter."

**"I will not see it!"**
The refrain of "The Spilled Blood," the second section of the "Lament," in which the speaker refuses to look at his friend's blood on the sand (also translated "I don't want to see it!"). The elegy continues with "The Laid-Out Body" and "Absent Soul," which tells the dead man "you have died forever." It ends "I sing of his elegance with words that groan, / and I remember a sad breeze through the olive trees."

**The House of Bernarda Alba**
Lorca's last play (1936), with an all-female cast and the third play of the Rural Trilogy. After her second husband's funeral, the tyrannical widow Bernarda imposes an eight-year mourning period and locks her five unmarried daughters inside the house. Her servant La Poncia warns her of the trouble brewing among them.

**Adela and Pepe el Romano**
The central conflict of The House of Bernarda Alba. Pepe el Romano is engaged to Angustias, the oldest and wealthiest daughter, but secretly meets the youngest, Adela, who defiantly wears a green dress. Bernarda fires her gun at Pepe, her daughter Martirio falsely says he is dead, and Adela hangs herself. Bernarda insists Adela died a virgin, orders that no one weep, and demands "Silence!"

**"Romance Sonámbulo" and "Green, how I want you green"**
Lorca's most famous lyric, the "Sleepwalking Ballad" from Gypsy Ballads. It opens "Green, how I want you green. / Green wind. Green branches. / The ship out on the sea / and the horse on the mountain," while a gypsy girl with green flesh, green hair, and "eyes of cold silver" dreams on her balcony.

**"I want to trade my horse for her house"**
Lines from "Romance Sonámbulo," spoken by a wounded young smuggler who asks an older friend to trade "my horse for her house, my saddle for her mirror, my knife for her blanket." The two friends climb toward the high balconies, but the girl is already dead, her body held "up above the water" of a cistern by "an icicle of moon."

**Gypsy Ballads (Romancero gitano)**
Lorca's popular 1928 collection of eighteen ballads (romances) about the Roma of Andalusia, which includes "Romance Sonámbulo." In "Ballad of the Moon, Moon," the moon comes to the forge and shows her breasts to a gypsy boy before carrying him away. Another ballad describes the arrest of Antoñito el Camborio, "brown as a green moon," carrying a willow rod on the road to Seville.

**The Rural Trilogy**
The name for Lorca's three tragedies of rural Andalusian life, Blood Wedding, Yerma, and The House of Bernarda Alba. They focus on frustrated passion, honor, and the restrictions placed on women, and are his best-known plays.

**Yerma**
The second play of the Rural Trilogy (1934). Its title character, whose name means "barren," longs for a child, but her husband Juan does not want one. She is drawn to the shepherd Víctor, is watched by her two sisters-in-law, visits the conjurer Dolores for a fertility ritual, and is gossiped about by washerwomen at a stream. At the end she strangles Juan and cries "I have killed my son!", since she can now never have a child.

**Poet in New York**
A surreal collection written during Lorca's 1929–1930 stay in New York, while he studied at Columbia, and published after his death. It reacts to the city's alienation, racism, and the 1929 stock market crash, and includes "Ode to Walt Whitman."

**"City That Does Not Sleep"**
A poem from Poet in New York (subtitled "Brooklyn Bridge Nocturne") that opens "In the sky there is nobody asleep. Nobody, nobody." It warns that "living iguanas will come and bite the men who do not dream" and declares "Life is not a dream. Careful! Careful! Careful!"

**Lorca's execution in 1936**
In August 1936, at the start of the Spanish Civil War, Lorca was arrested in Granada and shot by Nationalist forces, and his body was never found. A leading member of the Generation of '27, he became a symbol of the war's victims. Allen Ginsberg's "A Supermarket in California" asks "what were you doing down by the watermelons?" of him, and the Irish biographer Ian Gibson investigated his death.

**"Gacela of the Dark Death"**
A poem from Lorca's late collection The Tamarit Divan, modeled on Arabic and Persian ghazals. Its speaker says "I want to sleep the sleep of the apples, / far from the tumult of cemeteries."
